title: Processing a home pig for the freezer
subtitle: Preparing a carcass at home for your own consumption.
excerpt: Processing a pig at home is legal for meat for your own consumption in the UK. The carcass is split, chilled, and broken into primal cuts before further butchery into chops, roasting joints, and cubes for the freezer. A single pig of 60 to 80 kg deadweight gives 30 to 50 kg of usable meat.
sourceNotes: Carla Emery, Encyclopedia of Country Living (9th edn., 1994), pork butchery chapter. AHDB Pork, Retail Cutting Specifications (UK). Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall, River Cottage Meat Book (2004), pork chapter.

glossaryTerms.definition: The large sections a carcass is divided into before further butchery: loin, leg, shoulder, belly, and head.
The backbone. Splitting or removing the chine is one of the first steps in dividing a carcass into two sides.

aliases: cutting up a pig at home

content.text: Home processing of a pig for your own consumption does not require an abattoir licence. The pig must be killed humanely on the farm (vet-supervised or by a licensed slaughterman), then processed in clean conditions. Meat processed at home cannot be sold.

On-farm slaughter for own consumption is permitted under Regulation (EC) 853/2004 as implemented in the UK. The pig must be killed by a licensed slaughterman or under veterinary supervision. You must not sell, give away, or donate any of the meat; it must be consumed within your household.
Chilling the carcass

A freshly slaughtered pig carcass must cool to below 7 C at the deepest point (usually the haunch) within 24 hours, and be maintained there throughout processing. Work outdoors in cold weather (below 5 C ambient) or in a chiller if available. Do not process a carcass that has not been adequately chilled.
Splitting into sides
Hang the carcass from the gambrel hooks at the hind legs, head down. The backbone runs down the centre.
Split the
chine
with a saw, running down the centre of the backbone from the aitch-bone at the pelvis to the neck. A reciprocating saw with a long blade is easier than a handsaw for a first-timer.
Once split, each side (or half carcass) can be laid on a clean work surface for further butchery.
Breaking into primal cuts
From each half, cut the five main
primal cuts
before further butchery into freezer portions.
Leg (the whole hind quarter): saw through at the aitch-bone. A large roasting joint. Can be left whole for a leg ham or split into two smaller joints.
Loin (the back behind the shoulder): cut between the last rib and the loin. This section yields pork chops (cut across the bone), rack of pork, and tenderloin.
Belly (the underside): cut away from the loin and spare ribs. Yields pork belly for roasting and streaky bacon strips.
Shoulder: the front quarter forward of the third rib. Yields a bone-in shoulder for slow roasting, or boned and rolled for pork shoulder joints.
Spare ribs and neck: the ribs separate from the belly; the neck is a good braising joint or goes into mince.
Further butchery for the freezer
Use the boning knife to work closely against the bone when boning out joints. Keep the blade angled toward the bone rather than the meat to preserve the joint size.
Chops: saw or use the cleaver to cut across the loin at 2 to 3 cm intervals. Double chops (4 to 5 cm) are more forgiving to cook.
Wrap each piece tightly in cling film, then in freezer bags. Label with the cut name and date. Use within 6 months for best quality, though meat is safe for up to 12 months frozen.

attrs.title: Approximate yield from a 60 kg deadweight pig

content.text: Two legs: 10 to 14 kg
Two loins (inc. chops and tenderloin): 8 to 10 kg
Two bellies: 6 to 8 kg
Two shoulders: 8 to 12 kg
Back fat for lard: 2 to 4 kg

attrs.cue: Meat surface is sticky or has a slight sour smell after chilling overnight
attrs.cause: Carcass did not chill rapidly enough; bacterial surface activity starting
attrs.fix: Trim the surface layer from affected areas. Do not process further if there is deep discolouration or a strong smell. If in doubt, contact your local environmental health officer.

attrs.cue: Knife keeps slipping off the bone during boning
attrs.cause: Knife not sharp enough, or cutting at the wrong angle
attrs.fix: Sharpen the boning knife before each processing session. Angle the blade directly onto the bone surface and work in short strokes rather than long dragging cuts.
